title: Partition Shapes into Equal Parts
goal: I can find one whole, check equal shares, and name halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths.
catchAll: Find the whole. Check that the pieces cover equal areas. Count all the equal pieces to name them.

teacher.def: The denominator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are in the whole. It is the bottom part of the fraction
A unit fraction is ONE part of a whole. It always has a numerator of one.
The numerator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are being described. It is the top part of the fraction.
A fraction is a number used when a whole is split into equal parts.

glossary.whole: one complete shape, including every part inside its outside edge
glossary.equal: the same amount; equal shares of a shape cover the same area
glossary.area: how much flat space a piece covers

screens.title: Start with one whole
text: This complete strip is one whole.
Trace its outside edge; all the space inside belongs to the whole.

screens.title: Make parts of the whole
text: A part is a piece of the whole.
This line divides the strip into two pieces; the outside strip stays the same.

screens.title: Check equal shares
text: Equal shares cover the same amount of the whole.
These pieces have matching widths and heights, so neither covers more area.

screens.title: Two pieces can be unequal
text: Here the highlighted piece is wider and just as tall.
It covers more area, so these two pieces are not equal shares.

screens.title: 2 equal pieces: halves
text: 2 equal pieces together make this one whole.
Each piece is one half; all the pieces are called halves.

screens.title: 3 equal pieces: thirds
text: 3 equal pieces together make this one whole.
Each piece is one third; all the pieces are called thirds.

screens.title: 4 equal pieces: fourths
text: 4 equal pieces together make this one whole.
Each piece is one fourth; all the pieces are called fourths.

screens.title: 6 equal pieces: sixths
text: 6 equal pieces together make this one whole.
Each piece is one sixth; all the pieces are called sixths.

screens.title: 8 equal pieces: eighths
text: 8 equal pieces together make this one whole.
Each piece is one eighth; all the pieces are called eighths.

screens.title: Different cuts can make equal shares
text: This strip has a top half and a bottom half.
The two rows have matching widths and heights, so each is one half of the whole.

screens.title: Count the pieces, not just the color
text: The whole includes colored and uncolored pieces.

sections.heading: What comes first
sections.text: This first lesson begins with one complete shape before introducing its parts. Equal shares of a shape need equal area, not merely a particular number of pieces.

sections.heading: Use real paper
list: Point around the outside edge of one paper strip and call the complete strip the whole.
Fold it into two matching parts; match the pieces to check equal area.
Make another strip with one narrow piece and one wide piece; ask why two pieces are not automatically halves.
After the equal-area check, count all pieces to name halves, thirds, fourths, sixths or eighths.

sections.heading: What the diagrams show
sections.text: The strip examples compare pieces with equal heights, so matching widths establish matching areas. The circle examples use equal-angle wedges of the same circle. Color highlights a piece for comparison; it does not define the whole or make a piece larger.

sections.heading: The Lesson 7-1 learning journey
sections.text: Lesson 7-1 teaches each skill in three steps. I Do: a worked example, one step at a time, with the reason. We Do: a similar problem with a ? Help button and step-by-step guidance. You Do: a new problem with no hints; after two misses the lesson shows the worked example again, then your child tries again. The lesson opens one part at a time, so no teaching is skipped. It ends with a 10-question Final Check and a readiness report that keeps independent work apart from work done with help. Written answers need a grown-up to read them. The Learn It to Test steps here remain as optional extra practice.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to discuss
list: Counting only colored pieces instead of all pieces of the whole.
Calling any two pieces halves even when one piece is wider.
Using color, the number of cuts, or the number of pieces alone to decide whether areas are equal.

sections.heading: Reflect honestly
sections.text: The written response comes after concrete teaching and two mini-checks. A child or grown-up reviews the mathematical reasoning; the computer does not certify understanding from keywords or sentence length.
